tasks.story: Automated workflows — CRON schedules and database-event triggers — are dispatched by reading a workspace-side denormalized trigger table that is populated from the workspace copy of the workflow. As workflow data moves into core and those workspace writes are retired, that table would go blank and scheduled/event-driven workflows would silently stop firing for customers. The arc makes dispatch able to source its triggers from the core-derived trigger map instead, gated per workspace by a default-off feature flag so the switch can be rolled out tenant by tenant with identical firing behavior. It then repairs the drift-monitoring signal that gates that rollout, which was reporting permanent phantom drift for soft-deleted automated workflows while never inspecting the workspaces whose core mirror had failed entirely — making the one metric operators rely on to decide when flipping is safe untrustworthy in both directions.

tasks.story: Apps invoking an agent through the public agent-execution API could only hand it a single one-shot instruction string, so chat-style bots (Slack, Discord, Teams) had no way to pass the preceding thread history - each reply was produced with no memory of what had already been said in the conversation. Extend that public surface so a caller supplies either the single instruction string or an ordered array of user/assistant messages, mirroring the AI SDK's either-or shape, and enforce that exactly one of the two is provided. Thread the new shape through the shared application types, the API schema and SDK inputs and their regenerated clients, and the app-developer docs, while existing single-string callers keep working unchanged.

tasks.story: Anyone on the internet could hit the "forgot password" request endpoint unlimited times, so bots could pump password-reset emails at arbitrary addresses and spam people who never asked for a reset — it was the one email-taking auth mutation with no captcha in front of it. The same endpoint also told callers whether an address had an account, both in what it said (a found vs. not-found message) and in how long it took to answer, giving an easy way to harvest which emails are registered. Separately, requesting a new link could revoke a link the user already held if the write failed partway, leaving the user unable to recover their account. The arc gates the request behind a captcha, caps reset emails per address (3 per 15 minutes) with a clear rate-limit message, makes the response identical and equally fast whether or not the address exists, and keeps an already-issued link valid when rotation fails.
